The con- texts in which young people develop their understanding ofcivics and citizenship include the home, peer groups, schools and classrooms, and the wider community at the national and regional levels [ 30]. Sharing ideas and opinions with others through discussion can also be considered a formof societal participation [ 33]. Discussion is a central aspect of deliberative democracy, a process in which people from diverse backgrounds engage in dialogue and shared meaning-making to shape policies that will in uence their lives [ 34]. nodes.paragraph: But what exactly do we mean when we claim that knowledge is in crisis? To claim that knowledge is in crisis seems to imply that an opposite state of affairs, in which knowledge is not in crisis, can be true, or at least theoretically possible. But for knowledge not to be in crisis, a combination of factors must occur and it seems impossible for them all to happen at the same time: knowledge not in crisis is knowledge that is abundant but not excessive, easily accessible to all yet exhaustive and detailed; free from ideological and politi - cal influences; free from forces of various kinds that, vol - untarily or involuntarily, distort the narrative of facts and make them appear to be what they are not. Has there ever been such a moment in human history? It does not seem SO. So why speak of a crisis of knowledge today ? Is there some - thing in the current context, and especially in the context of contemporary liberal democracies, that makes knowledge seem to be in a particular state of crisis?

Toward a Criti - cal Ethics of Digital Capitalism, Giuseppe De Ruvo illus - trates the limits of algorithmic implementation and raises questions about their only supposed objectivity. First, the paper questions what an algorithm is, which it defines as an abstract machine consisting of a complex set of impera - tive, defined, finite rules that must perform a specific cal - culation efficiently. But what does an algorithm actually do? Algorithms perform calculations, and those calcula - tions also involve making predictions. The more complex the contexts, the less accurate and realistic the calculations performed by algorithms can be, even though they are pre - sented as tools that produce objective results and cannot make mistakes.
